\chapter{Bringing, Getting, Playing, Waiting}
\label{ch:la-getting-and-waiting-verbs}
\hlchaptermodality{42}

\begin{chapteropening}
\textbf{By the end of this chapter:} \emph{I can say I bring, I get, I play and I wait in Latin, produce the he-or-she form of each, and say whether a verb is welded together from two roots, built from a prefix on an older verb, or of ancestry nobody has settled.}

The chapter closes on exspectō: after learning it the reader produces all four first-person forms and all four third-person forms in sequence — ferō, accipiō, lūdō, exspectō and fert, accipit, lūdit, exspectat — sorts a verb's children from its siblings (expect against spectacle), and reaches back five chapters to retrieve videō and dō, neither of which had been revisited since chapter 37.
\end{chapteropening}

\section[ferō, ferre]{ferō — one verb, two ancestors}

\label{lesson:LA-C42-fero}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Claudō} shut the door that \textbf{aperiō} opened, and its root named a hook. This verb is stranger: it is not one word at all.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: ferō — \textquotedblleft{}I bring\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Ferō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I carry},\textquotedblright{} and so also \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I bring}\textquotedblright{} and \textquotedblleft{}I bear.\textquotedblright{} The dictionary form is \textbf{ferre}, not the \emph{-ere} you would expect.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{ferō} — I bring
  \item \textbf{fers} — you bring, to one person
  \item \textbf{fert} — he brings, she brings
  \item \textbf{ferimus} — we bring
  \item \textbf{fertis} — you bring, to several people
  \item \textbf{ferunt} — they bring
\end{itemize}

Say \textbf{fers} and \textbf{fert} slowly. Every verb so far put a vowel between the stem and the ending — \emph{claudis}, \emph{claudit}. Here the ending is jammed straight onto \emph{fer-}. That happens in the \emph{s}, \emph{t} and \emph{r} forms only; \textbf{ferimus} and \textbf{ferunt} keep their vowel.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Ferre} comes from Proto-Indo-European \emph{\textbf{*b\textsuperscript{h}er-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to carry.\textquotedblright{} English inherited that root directly, as the verb \textbf{bear} — so \emph{ferō} and \emph{bear} are blood relatives, not borrowings.

Now the odd part. To say \textquotedblleft{}I brought,\textquotedblright{} a Roman said \textbf{tulī}; the participle was \textbf{lātum}. Neither is from \emph{*b\textsuperscript{h}er-}: both come from \emph{\textbf{*telh\textsubscript{2}-}}, \textquotedblleft{}to lift.\textquotedblright{} One verb, two ancestries, welded together because each root had gone missing where the other survived. Grammarians call this \textbf{suppletion}, and you met a smaller case: \textbf{sum}, \textquotedblleft{}I am,\textquotedblright{} takes its past from another root.

Both halves are generous. From \emph{ferre}: \textbf{transfer} (carry across), \textbf{refer}, \textbf{prefer}, \textbf{confer}, \textbf{offer}, \textbf{suffer} (bear from under), and \textbf{fertile}, a field that carries a crop. \textbf{Differ} is \emph{dis-} plus \emph{ferre}, \textquotedblleft{}to carry apart\textquotedblright{} — and \textbf{defer} is that same Latin word split into two English ones. From \emph{lātum}: \textbf{relate} and \textbf{translate}.

Set this beside \textbf{dō}, \textquotedblleft{}I give.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Dō} hands a thing over; \emph{ferō} carries it.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ferō, fers, fert\textquotedblright{} — I bring, you bring, he or she brings
  \item \textquotedblleft{}ferimus, fertis, ferunt\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the two past pieces from the other root — tulī, lātum
  \item the giving verb beside the carrying one — dō, ferō
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I bring\textquotedblright{}, and \textquotedblleft{}he brings\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Ferō}, \textbf{fert}.) Which two forms keep a vowel before the ending? (\textbf{Ferimus} and \textbf{ferunt}.) How many roots make this verb, and what is that called? (\textbf{Two} — \emph{*b\textsuperscript{h}er-} and \emph{*telh\textsubscript{2}-}; \textbf{suppletion}.) Which English verb is the same word as \emph{ferō} by inheritance? (\textbf{Bear}.) Which earlier verb means \textquotedblleft{}I give\textquotedblright{}, and which means \textquotedblleft{}I close\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Dō}, and \textbf{claudō}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[accipiō, obtineō]{accipiō and obtineō — getting, two ways}

\label{lesson:LA-C42-accipio}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Ferō} carried a thing toward somebody. These two verbs are what happens at the other end — and neither is a new word. Each is a prefix welded onto a verb you have.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: accipiō — \textquotedblleft{}I receive\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Accipiō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I receive},\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}I get,\textquotedblright{} \textquotedblleft{}I accept.\textquotedblright{} Latin has no all-purpose verb for English \emph{get}; it uses the precise one.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{accipiō} — I receive
  \item \textbf{accipis} — you receive, to one person
  \item \textbf{accipit} — he receives, she receives
  \item \textbf{accipimus} — we receive
  \item \textbf{accipitis} — you receive, to several people
  \item \textbf{accipiunt} — they receive
\end{itemize}

Those endings should feel familiar: they are \textbf{capiō}'s, because \emph{capiō} is what is inside this word.

\subsection*{You'll want to know: obtineō — \textquotedblleft{}I get hold of\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Obtineō} is the other half of \textquotedblleft{}get\textquotedblright{}: not \emph{receive} but \emph{acquire and keep} — getting hold of a thing and holding it. It is \textbf{second conjugation}, \emph{-ēre}: \textbf{obtineō, obtinēs, obtinet, obtinēmus, obtinētis, obtinent}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{Accipere} is \emph{ad}, \textquotedblleft{}to, toward,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{capere}, \textquotedblleft{}to take.\textquotedblright{} Take it toward yourself, and you have received it. Two things happened at the seam. The \emph{d} of \emph{ad} turned into the \emph{c} it was leaning on — \textbf{ad-capere} becoming \textbf{accipere}. And the \emph{a} of \emph{capere}, now buried in a longer word, thinned to \emph{i}. English \textbf{accept} and \textbf{acceptance} come from here.

\textbf{Obtinēre} is \emph{ob}, \textquotedblleft{}over against,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{tenēre}, \textquotedblleft{}to hold.\textquotedblright{} The same vowel thinning shows: not \emph{ob-tenēre} but \textbf{obtinēre}. English took it whole as \textbf{obtain}.

Now put \textbf{adiuvō} next to them. It is \emph{ad} plus \emph{iuvāre} — the same \emph{ad}, sitting in front of a vowel, where it had nothing to lean on and so stayed itself. One prefix, two states: kept in \emph{adiuvō}, swallowed in \emph{accipiō}.

Two flags. English \textbf{receive} is from \emph{recipere}, a different prefix on the same verb. And \textbf{retain} and \textbf{contain} belong to \emph{tenēre} at large, not to \emph{obtinēre}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}accipiō, accipis, accipit\textquotedblright{} — I, you, he or she receives
  \item \textquotedblleft{}obtineō, obtinēs, obtinet\textquotedblright{} — I, you, he or she gets hold of
  \item the verb inside each one — capiō, and the hold-verb tenēre
  \item the prefix in three states — adiuvō, accipiō, obtineō
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I receive\textquotedblright{}, and \textquotedblleft{}they receive\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Accipiō}, \textbf{accipiunt}.) Which verb is buried inside it, and what happened to that verb's \emph{a}? (\textbf{Capiō}; it \textbf{thinned to \emph{i}}.) What are the two pieces of \emph{obtinēre}? (\emph{\textbf{Ob}} and \emph{\textbf{tenēre}}, \textquotedblleft{}to hold.\textquotedblright{}) Which earlier verb shows the same \emph{ad-} unswallowed? (\textbf{Adiuvō}.) And which verb means \textquotedblleft{}I bring\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Ferō}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[lūdō, lūdere]{lūdō — playing, and being played}

\label{lesson:LA-C42-ludo}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Accipiō} and \textbf{obtineō} were built out of older parts. This verb is the opposite case: a short word whose own parentage is unknown, and which still went on to father a crowd.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: lūdō — \textquotedblleft{}I play\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Lūdō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I play}\textquotedblright{} — a game, a sport, an instrument, a part on stage. The dictionary form is \textbf{lūdere}, with a long \emph{ū} and a short \emph{e}.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{lūdō} — I play
  \item \textbf{lūdis} — you play, to one person
  \item \textbf{lūdit} — he plays, she plays
  \item \textbf{lūdimus} — we play
  \item \textbf{lūditis} — you play, to several people
  \item \textbf{lūdunt} — they play
\end{itemize}

Third conjugation, the short \emph{-ere} group — the endings of \emph{claudō}.

\begin{cousinweb}
Begin with the honest limit. Where \emph{lūdere} came from before Latin is \textbf{not settled}. Dictionaries offer a root along the lines of \emph{*loid-}, \textquotedblleft{}play,\textquotedblright{} but specialists disagree about its form and about whether the Greek word usually cited belongs at all. Some sources state a root confidently; they are more confident than the evidence.

The noun is \textbf{lūdus}, and it means two things at once: a \textbf{game}, and a \textbf{school}. The elementary school where a Roman child learned letters was the \emph{lūdus litterārius} — the place you went to \textbf{legō} and \textbf{scrībō}, called by the word for play. Both senses sit in the one Latin word.

The English harvest is almost all about deception, because \emph{lūdere} also meant \textquotedblleft{}to make sport of.\textquotedblright{} \textbf{Illusion} is \emph{in-} plus the root: a playing-upon. \textbf{Delude} plays you down, \textbf{elude} plays you away, \textbf{allude} plays toward a thing without naming it, and to \textbf{collude} is to play together against someone. \textbf{Ludicrous} kept the plain sense — fit for a game. A \textbf{prelude} plays before, an \textbf{interlude} between.

Two flags. English \textbf{play} is Germanic and is no relation. And the board game \textbf{Ludo}, sold in Britain from the 1890s, is named with exactly the form you just said: \emph{lūdō}, \textquotedblleft{}I play.\textquotedblright{}
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lūdō, lūdis, lūdit\textquotedblright{} — I play, you play, he or she plays
  \item \textquotedblleft{}lūdimus, lūditis, lūdunt\textquotedblright{} — we, you all, they
  \item the two things a lūdus was — a game, and a school
  \item what you did at that school — legō, scrībō
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
How does Latin say \textquotedblleft{}I play\textquotedblright{}, and \textquotedblleft{}they play\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Lūdō}, \textbf{lūdunt}.) Is this verb's older ancestry known? (\textbf{No} — it is unsettled, whatever a confident dictionary says.) What were the two senses of \emph{lūdus}, and which two earlier verbs happened at the second one? (\textbf{Game} and \textbf{school}; \textbf{legō} and \textbf{scrībō}.) Which English word means a playing-upon? (\textbf{Illusion}.) And which verb means \textquotedblleft{}I receive\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Accipiō}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
\section[exspectō, exspectāre]{exspectō — waiting is looking out}

\label{lesson:LA-C42-exspecto}



\begin{quote}
\textbf{Lūdō} was a plain word with an unknown parent. This last verb of the chapter is the reverse: you can see straight through it to its two pieces.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: exspectō — \textquotedblleft{}I wait\textquotedblright{}}
\textbf{Exspectō} means \textquotedblleft{}\textbf{I wait},\textquotedblright{} and more exactly \textquotedblleft{}I wait \emph{for}\textquotedblright{} — it usually has an object. It is \textbf{first conjugation}, the \emph{-āre} group.

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textbf{exspectō} — I wait
  \item \textbf{exspectās} — you wait, to one person
  \item \textbf{exspectat} — he waits, she waits
  \item \textbf{exspectāmus} — we wait
  \item \textbf{exspectātis} — you wait, to several people
  \item \textbf{exspectant} — they wait
\end{itemize}

Romans wrote it both \textbf{exspectō} and \emph{expectō}, since only one \emph{s} was ever pronounced. The longer spelling is the one that shows the seam, so it is the one worth learning.

\begin{cousinweb}
\emph{Exspectāre} is \emph{ex}, \textquotedblleft{}out,\textquotedblright{} plus \emph{spectāre}, \textquotedblleft{}to watch.\textquotedblright{} To wait is to \textbf{look out for}. And \emph{spectāre} is itself built: it is the over-and-over form of \emph{specere}, \textquotedblleft{}to look\textquotedblright{} — so the middle piece already means \textquotedblleft{}keep looking.\textquotedblright{}

English \textbf{expect} is the direct child. Be careful with the rest. \textbf{Spectacle}, \textbf{spectator}, \textbf{inspect}, \textbf{respect} and \textbf{suspect} are not from \emph{exspectāre}; they are its brothers and sisters, the same \emph{spectāre} with other prefixes on the front. Saying they come \emph{from} \textquotedblleft{}expect\textquotedblright{} gets the family tree upside down.

Set this beside \textbf{videō}, \textquotedblleft{}I see.\textquotedblright{} \emph{Videō} is a wholly different root, and its English children — \textbf{vision}, \textbf{video}, \textbf{evident} — are a separate family. Latin had one word for the eye receiving a thing and another for the eye going out after it.

One good flag. English \textbf{wait} looks Romance, because it reached English through French. It is not. It is a Germanic word the French had borrowed first, and its true relatives are \textbf{watch} and \textbf{wake}.
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{Your turn}
Say these aloud:

\begin{itemize}
\raggedright
  \item \textquotedblleft{}exspectō, exspectās, exspectat\textquotedblright{} — I, you, he or she waits
  \item this chapter's four \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms — ferō, accipiō, lūdō, exspectō
  \item the four \textquotedblleft{}he or she\textquotedblright{} forms — fert, accipit, lūdit, exspectat
  \item the two eye-verbs — videō, exspectō
\end{itemize}

\begin{tcolorbox}[breakable,colback=teal!4,colframe=teal!35!black,title={Before you move on}]
Give the chapter's four \textquotedblleft{}I\textquotedblright{} forms, then the four \textquotedblleft{}he or she\textquotedblright{} forms. (\textbf{Ferō, accipiō, lūdō, exspectō}; \textbf{fert, accipit, lūdit, exspectat}.) What does \emph{exspectāre} literally say? (\textbf{Look out} — \emph{ex} plus \emph{spectāre}.) Is \textbf{spectacle} a child of \emph{exspectāre}? (\textbf{No} — a sibling, from \emph{spectāre} directly.) Which verb is welded from two roots, and which two are prefix plus an older verb? (\textbf{Ferō}; \textbf{accipiō} and \textbf{obtineō}.) Which verb's own ancestry is unknown, and which earlier verb means \textquotedblleft{}I see\textquotedblright{}? (\textbf{Lūdō}; and \textbf{videō}.)
\end{tcolorbox}
